solution:
\(\vec{F} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B}) = q\vec{v}\times(B\hat{i} + B\hat{j} + B_0\hat{k})\)
Given, \(q = 1\), \(\vec{v} = 2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{F} = 4\hat{i} - 20\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}\)
\(\Rightarrow (4\hat{i} - 20\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}) = (2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 6\hat{k})\times(B\hat{i} + B\hat{j} + B_0\hat{k})\)
Thus, calculating values of RHS,
\(\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ 2 & 4 & 6\\ B & B & B_0\end{vmatrix}\)
\(\Rightarrow \hat{i}(4B_0 - 6B) - \hat{j}(2B_0 - 6B) + \hat{k}(2B - 4B)\)
Comparing L.H.S and R.H.S,
\(4B_0 - 6B = 4 \Rightarrow 2B_0 - 3B = 2\) ...(1)
\(-(2B_0 - 6B) = -20 \Rightarrow B_0 - 3B = 10\) ...(2)
\(2B - 4B = 12 \Rightarrow B = -6\) ...(3)
From (2) and (3)
\(B = -6\) and \(B_0 = -8\)
Hence, \(\vec{B} = -6\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} - 8\hat{k}\)

The wire has two straight semi-infinite parts and a semicircle of radius \(R\) centred at \(P\).
Each straight semi-infinite part ends level with \(P\), so each gives \(\frac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi R}\) at \(P\), into the page (\(\otimes\)). Together they give \(\frac{\mu_0 i}{2\pi R}\) into the page.
The semicircle gives \(\frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}\) at its centre, out of the page (\(\odot\)).
\( B_{net} = \frac{\mu_0 i}{4R} - \frac{\mu_0 i}{2\pi R} = \frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}\left[1 - \frac{2}{\pi}\right] \), pointed away from the page.

The centre O is fixed, so the centre of mass of the disc is at rest and the disc's total linear momentum is zero.
For a body with zero linear momentum, the angular momentum is the same about every point: \(\vec{L}_P = \vec{L}_O + \vec{r}_{OP} \times \vec{p} = \vec{L}_O\).
So \(L_A = L_B = I\omega = \dfrac{MR^2}{2}\omega\), whatever the distances OA and OB.
\(\dfrac{L_A}{L_B} = 1\).

\(\vec{P_1} + \vec{P_2} = mv\sin\theta\,\hat{i} - mv\cos\theta\,\hat{j} + (-mv\sin\theta\,\hat{i} - mv\cos\theta\,\hat{j})\). \(P_{Total} = |\vec{P_1} + \vec{P_2}| = 2mv\cos\theta\). At \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(P_{Total} = 0\); at \(\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(P_{Total} = 0\); at \(\theta = 0\), \(P_{Total\,max} = 2mV\). So the graph is a dome (option C).

A concave lens is a diverging lens. A ray parallel to the principal axis is spread out by the lens so that, after refraction, it appears to come from a point on the axis on the same side as the incoming light.
NCERT names this point the first principal focus \(F\): a ray parallel to the principal axis passes through the second principal focus \(F'\) of a convex lens, or appears to diverge from the first principal focus \(F\) of a concave lens.
So the ray appears to diverge from the first principal focus.

Given \(i = 60^\circ\) and \(\mu = \sqrt{3}\).
By Snell's law, \(\sin 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}\sin r\), so \(\sin r = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}/2}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(r = 30^\circ\).
The reflected ray makes \(60^\circ\) with the normal on the incident side and the refracted ray makes \(30^\circ\) with the normal on the other side.
Angle between them \(= 180^\circ - 60^\circ - 30^\circ = 90^\circ\).
(This is the polarising angle: \(\tan i = \mu\) gives \(i = 60^\circ\), and at that angle the reflected and refracted rays are always perpendicular.)

Applying Kepler's 3rd law: \(T^2 \propto R^3\). Radius of Martian orbit \(R' = 4R\). \(\left(\frac{T'}{T}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{R'}{R}\right)^3 = \left(\frac{4R}{R}\right)^3 = 4^3 = 64 \Rightarrow \frac{T'}{T} = 8\). Length of 1 year on Mercury \(= T = \frac{T'}{8} = \frac{687}{8} = 85.88\) days. The question says the radius is only about 4 times, so the answer is about 86 days, and the nearest option is 88 earth days.

\( Mg' = Mg\dfrac{R^2}{(R+h)^2} \)
At \( A \) (height \(2R\)): \( Mg' = Mg\dfrac{R^2}{(R+2R)^2} = \dfrac{Mg}{9} \)
At \( B \) (height \(\frac{3R}{2}\)): \( Mg' = Mg\dfrac{R^2}{\left(R+\frac{3R}{2}\right)^2} = \dfrac{4Mg}{25} \)
Change in weight \( = Mg\left(\dfrac{4}{25} - \dfrac{1}{9}\right) = Mg\dfrac{11}{225} \).
Taking \(g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2\): \( = 100 \times 10 \times \dfrac{11}{225} \approx 48.9 \approx 49 \) N.

Energy of incident radiation = 2.20 eV. Work function of Cs \( \to \) 2.14 eV, Work function of K \( \to \) 2.30 eV, Work function of Na \( \to \) 2.75 eV. A surface emits photoelectrons only if the photon energy is more than its work function. 2.20 eV is more than 2.14 eV but less than 2.30 eV and 2.75 eV, so only caesium may emit photoelectrons.

At any point of time, \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}\). Here \(m\) is decreasing, so the time period \(T\) decreases and \(\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\) increases.
The sand that leaks out moves with the box as it leaves, so it carries away its own kinetic energy. Averaged over a cycle, a small mass \(dm\) carries away energy \(dm \cdot \frac{1}{4}\omega^2A^2 = \frac{E}{2m}\,dm\), where \(E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2\).
So \(\frac{dE}{E} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{dm}{m}\), which gives \(E \propto \sqrt{m}\). With \(k\) fixed, \(\frac{1}{2}kA^2 = E\) gives \(A \propto m^{1/4}\), so the amplitude decreases as the sand leaks out.
So \(\omega(t)\) increases and \(A(t)\) decreases.

According to the modified Ampere's law, \(\oint B \cdot dl = \mu_0(I_C + I_D)\).
In the wires the current is a conduction current, \(I_C = I\). In the gap between the plates no charge flows, so \(I_C = 0\), but the electric field there grows as the plates charge, giving a displacement current \(I_D = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = I\).
So the current is the same all round the circuit: in the gap a displacement current equal to \(I\) flows, in the same direction as \(I\).

\( \dfrac{\mu_r}{\varepsilon_r} = \dfrac{1}{4} \)
\( \dfrac{E}{H} = \dfrac{E\mu}{B} = v\mu = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}}\mu = \sqrt{\dfrac{\mu}{\varepsilon}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\mu_0\mu_r}{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon_0}}\sqrt{\dfrac{\mu_r}{\varepsilon_r}} = 120\pi\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 60\pi \)
So \(E : H = 60\pi : 1\).

On a P-V graph the slope of an isothermal is \(\dfrac{dP}{dV} = -\dfrac{P}{V}\) and the slope of an adiabatic is \(\dfrac{dP}{dV} = -\gamma\dfrac{P}{V}\). Since \(\gamma > 1\), the adiabatic falls more steeply than the isothermal.
From the common starting point, the isobaric curve is horizontal and the isochoric curve is vertical. The adiabatic therefore lies between the isothermal and the isochoric.
In the figure that is curve 2.

Diamond: each carbon is (sp^3) hybridised and bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional covalent network. It is the hardest natural substance and cannot be used as a lubricant.
Graphite: each carbon is (sp^2) hybridised and bonded to three others in flat hexagonal layers. The layers are held by weak van der Waals forces and slide over each other, so graphite is used as a dry lubricant.
So (A) is wrong (diamond is a 3-D network, graphite is layered), (B) is wrong (both are covalent), (D) is wrong (only graphite is a lubricant), and (C) is correct.

Down group 13 the poor shielding of the inner d and f electrons holds the (ns^2) pair tightly, so it takes less and less part in bonding (the inert pair effect). The +1 state therefore becomes more stable down the group.
In thallium the +1 state is the main one and Tl(III) is a strong oxidising agent, so (TlI) is more stable than (TlI_3): (D) is correct, and (A) is reversed.
For aluminium +3 is by far the stable state, so (C) is wrong.
Note: for indium the +3 state is still the more stable one, so (B) also reads as true; the official key is (D).

Assertion A is true: helium is used to dilute oxygen in modern diving apparatus.
The reason it is used is its very low solubility in blood, so it does not dissolve in the diver's blood under pressure.
Reason R is taken as true because helium and oxygen mix freely in all proportions, but that is not why helium is chosen.
So both A and R are true, and R is not the correct explanation of A: (B).

Degree of unsaturation (= (8+1) - dfrac{8}{2} = 5): a benzene ring (4) and one C=O.
A red orange precipitate with 2,4-DNP shows an aldehyde or a ketone.
No reduction of Fehling's reagent: P is a ketone, or an aromatic aldehyde, since aromatic aldehydes do not respond to Fehling's test.
If P is acetophenone, (	ext{C}_6	ext{H}_5	ext{COCH}_3), drastic oxidation with chromic acid gives benzoic acid, Q, which gives (	ext{CO}_2) with (	ext{NaHCO}_3): option (D).
If P is 4-methylbenzaldehyde, p-(	ext{CH}_3	ext{C}_6	ext{H}_4	ext{CHO}), drastic oxidation turns both the CHO and the (	ext{CH}_3) group into COOH, giving terephthalic acid, which also gives (	ext{CO}_2) with (	ext{NaHCO}_3): option (C).
So both (C) and (D) fit the data, and the official key accepts (C) or (D).

\(2\text{KMnO}_4 \xrightarrow{513\ \text{K}} \text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4 + \text{MnO}_2 + \text{O}_2\)
Check: K 2 = 2; Mn 2 = 1 + 1; O 8 = 4 + 2 + 2.
\(\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4\), potassium manganate, is green. Manganese in it is +6 (\(3d^1\)), with one unpaired electron, so it is paramagnetic. Hence (A).

\(\text{R-CN} \xrightarrow{\text{(i) LiAlH}_4,\ \text{(ii) H}_2\text{O}} \text{R-CH}_2\text{-NH}_2\) (A)
\(\text{R-CN} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2\text{/Ni}} \text{R-CH}_2\text{-NH}_2\) (C)
\(\text{R-CN} \xrightarrow{\text{Na(Hg)/C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}} \text{R-CH}_2\text{-NH}_2\) (D)
Sn + HCl is the reagent for reducing a nitro compound, not a nitrile (B). A nitrile with \(\text{SnCl}_2\) and HCl, then water, gives an aldehyde (Stephen reaction), not an amine.
\(\text{Br}_2\)/aq. NaOH is the Hoffmann bromamide reagent: it acts on an amide, not a nitrile (E).
So A, C and D reduce nitriles to primary amines.

\[\ln K_1 = \ln A - \frac{E_a}{RT_1}\ \ldots(i)\]
\[\ln K_2 = \ln A - \frac{E_a}{RT_2}\ \ldots(ii)\]
(ii) − (i)
\[\ln\frac{K_2}{K_1} = \frac{E_a}{R}\left[\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right]\]
\[\ln\frac{0.14}{0.04} = \frac{E_a}{R}\left[\frac{700 - 500}{500 \times 700}\right]\]
\[\log 3.5 = \frac{E_a}{2.303 \times R}\left[\frac{1}{250 \times 7}\right]\]
\[0.5441 = \frac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.31}\left[\frac{1}{250 \times 7}\right]\]
